title: Berkshire 2006 letter: Buffett on float, incentives, temperament, newspapers and the 2-and-20 folly
summary: Buffett's 2006 letter covers insurance float and disciplined super-cat pricing, buying businesses from owners who want a permanent home, simple performance-tied CEO pay, the decline of newspapers, truly independent directors, and the cost of Wall Street fees. It also describes the temperament he wants in a successor investor.

principles.text: Float is money you hold but don't own; its cost over time should be below industry norms, even zero or less, though bad years will come.
principles.quote: Simply put, float is money we hold that is not ours but which we get to invest.

principles.text: Only take insurance risk when paid appropriately; underpriced risk guarantees eventual losses, even if any single year looks fine.
principles.quote: Appropriate prices don’t guarantee profits in any given year, but inappropriate prices most certainly guarantee eventual losses.

principles.text: Be fearful when others are greedy and greedy when others are fearful, in insurance pricing as in markets.
principles.quote: Our behavior here parallels that which we employ in financial markets: Be fearful when others are greedy, and be greedy when others are fearful.

principles.text: Great managers matter, but a business with eroding fundamentals eventually overwhelms even brilliant management; pick good businesses.
principles.quote: When an industry’s underlying economics are crumbling, talented management may slow the rate of decline. Eventually, though, eroding fundamentals will overwhelm managerial brilliance.

principles.text: Tie CEO incentives to results the CEO controls, not to unrelated Berkshire-wide outcomes or market swings.
principles.quote: We issue no lottery tickets that carry payoffs unrelated to business performance.

principles.text: A top investor needs temperament and risk sense, not just brains or a recent record: independent thinking, emotional stability, understanding of behavior.
principles.quote: Independent thinking, emotional stability, and a keen understanding of both human and institutional behavior is vital to long-term investment success.
